body:
Earthquakes as endogenic processes

The surface of the Earth is continuously modified by forces originating both within and outside it. Forces originating within the Earth are called endogenic forces, while processes operating at or near its surface, such as weathering and erosion, are called exogenic processes.

Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are important manifestations of endogenic activity. They can rapidly modify the landscape, whereas processes such as mountain building generally operate over much longer periods.

An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the Earth caused by the release of accumulated energy within it. This energy travels through the Earth in the form of seismic waves.

How a tectonic earthquake occurs

The lithosphere consists of the crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates that move slowly relative to one another. Their movements generate stress in rocks, particularly along plate boundaries and existing faults.

A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures in rocks along which displacement has occurred. Friction may temporarily prevent movement along a fault even while tectonic forces continue to act. As stress accumulates, the rocks deform and store elastic energy.

When the accumulated stress becomes sufficient to overcome resistance, the rocks suddenly slip along the fault. Part of the stored energy is released as seismic waves. This basic explanation of earthquake generation is known as the elastic rebound theory.

Focus and epicentre

  • Focus or hypocentre: The point inside the Earth where earthquake rupture begins.
  • Epicentre: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
  • Focal depth: The vertical distance between the focus and the Earth's surface.
  • Seismic waves: Vibrations carrying energy away from the earthquake source.

Ground shaking is frequently severe near the epicentre, particularly during shallow earthquakes. However, the epicentre is not necessarily the location of maximum damage. Local geology, soil conditions, the extent of fault rupture and building quality influence the actual pattern of destruction.

Classification according to focal depth

Earthquake typeApproximate focal depth
Shallow-focus0–70 km
Intermediate-focus70–300 km
Deep-focus300–700 km

Most earthquakes are shallow. At comparable magnitudes and surface distances, shallow earthquakes generally produce stronger surface shaking than deep earthquakes. Intermediate and deep earthquakes occur mainly within descending tectonic plates at subduction zones.

Classification according to cause

  • Tectonic earthquakes: Result from sudden displacement along faults and constitute the most common category.
  • Volcanic earthquakes: Associated with magma movement, pressure changes and rock fracturing in volcanic regions.
  • Collapse earthquakes: Small earthquakes associated with the collapse of underground cavities or mines.
  • Explosion earthquakes: Seismic disturbances produced by large explosions.
  • Reservoir-induced earthquakes: Earthquakes that may result when reservoir loading and water penetration alter stresses and fluid pressure along existing faults.

Human activities such as mining, fluid injection and reservoir impoundment can induce seismicity under suitable geological conditions. The existence of a reservoir does not mean that an earthquake will necessarily occur.

The Bhuj earthquake

The destructive earthquake of 26 January 2001 in the Kachchh region of Gujarat demonstrated that major tectonic earthquakes can occur within continental plates, away from their immediate boundaries.

Prelims focus

  • Focus and hypocentre are synonymous.
  • The epicentre lies vertically above the focus.
  • Tectonic earthquakes are the most common type.
  • Deep-focus earthquakes are mainly associated with subduction zones.
  • The Bhuj earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001.
  • Trap: The epicentre is not the underground point where rupture begins.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 12–14; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 19–22; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapters 10 and 13; US Geological Survey, Determining the Depth of an Earthquake; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Earthquake. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026. Source-access limitation: some indexed GPSC Books extracts were unreadable; accessible published textbook copies and official scientific references were used instead.]

body:
Body waves and surface waves

The energy released during an earthquake travels through the Earth as seismic waves. These waves are classified into body waves and surface waves according to the region through which they propagate.

Body waves travel through the Earth's interior and consist of primary waves and secondary waves. Their interaction with near-surface materials generates surface waves, which travel mainly along the Earth's surface.

Primary waves

Primary waves, or P-waves, are the fastest seismic waves. They produce alternating compression and expansion of the material through which they travel.

The particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation. P-waves are therefore longitudinal or compressional waves. They can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

Secondary waves

Secondary waves, or S-waves, travel more slowly than P-waves. They produce shearing motion in which particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

S-waves require a medium capable of resisting shear deformation. They travel through solids but cannot propagate as shear waves through liquids or gases.

Surface waves

Surface waves generally arrive after the body waves. Their motion is concentrated near the Earth's surface, where buildings and infrastructure are located. Their large amplitudes and prolonged shaking can make them especially destructive.

The two principal types of surface waves are:

  • Love waves: Produce horizontal side-to-side motion perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
  • Rayleigh waves: Produce rolling, approximately elliptical particle motion involving both vertical and horizontal displacement.

Comparison of seismic waves

PropertyP-wavesS-wavesSurface waves
CategoryBodyBodySurface
ArrivalFirstSecondGenerally last
MotionCompressionShearingRolling or lateral
Travel through liquidsYesNoNot body waves

Seismic shadow zones

Seismic waves change their speed and direction when they encounter materials with different physical properties. Their behaviour includes reflection, in which waves return from a boundary, and refraction, in which their paths bend.

A seismic shadow zone is a region where particular direct seismic waves from an earthquake are not detected because of the structure of the Earth's interior.

In the standard school-level representation, the angular distance is measured from the epicentre around the Earth's surface:

  • Within approximately 105 degrees: Both direct P-waves and S-waves can be received.
  • Between approximately 105 and 145 degrees: The direct P-wave shadow zone occurs because P-waves are strongly refracted at the core-mantle boundary. Direct S-waves are also absent.
  • Beyond approximately 145 degrees: P-waves refracted through the core can be recorded again, but direct S-waves remain absent.

The S-wave shadow zone extends beyond approximately 105 degrees and is therefore much larger than the P-wave shadow zone. These angular limits are rounded textbook values.

The inability of S-waves to pass through the outer core provides important evidence that the outer core is liquid. The passage and refraction of P-waves provide additional evidence about the Earth's internal structure.

The mantle is predominantly solid, although some regions deform slowly over geological time. Its ability to transmit S-waves distinguishes it from the liquid outer core.

Prelims focus

  • P-waves are longitudinal and travel through solids, liquids and gases.
  • S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids.
  • Love waves produce horizontal shearing motion.
  • Rayleigh waves produce rolling ground motion.
  • The conventional P-wave shadow zone lies between approximately 105 and 145 degrees.
  • Trap: The Earth's entire mantle is not molten.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 19–23, particularly Earthquake Waves and Emergence of Shadow Zone; US Geological Survey, About the Seismograms. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Seismic Waves and Evidence about the Earth's Interior

body:
Seismic instruments and records

A seismometer is an instrument that detects and measures ground motion. A seismograph is an instrument or recording system that records seismic motion. The resulting record is called a seismogram.

Because P-waves travel faster than S-waves, they generally arrive first at a seismic recording station. The difference between their arrival times increases with distance from the earthquake source. Records from multiple stations help scientists determine the earthquake's location, depth and magnitude.

Earthquake magnitude

Magnitude represents the overall size of an earthquake at its source. It is calculated using instrumental observations and is related to the energy released during the event.

Richter magnitude scale

The Richter scale, developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935, is a logarithmic scale originally designed for measuring local earthquakes. It uses the amplitude of recorded seismic waves, adjusted for distance.

  • An increase of 1 magnitude unit represents a 10-fold increase in the corresponding measured wave amplitude on the Richter scale.
  • An increase of 1 magnitude unit corresponds approximately to 32 times as much energy release.
  • A magnitude 7 earthquake releases approximately 1,000 times as much energy as a magnitude 5 earthquake.

Magnitude is not a percentage or a linear measurement. The Richter scale does not have a fixed upper limit of 10.

Moment magnitude scale

The moment magnitude scale, represented by Mw, is based on the seismic moment of an earthquake. Seismic moment depends on the area of fault rupture, the amount of displacement and the rigidity of the rocks involved.

Moment magnitude provides a more reliable description of the size of very large earthquakes than the original Richter scale. It is widely used for reporting major earthquakes.

Earthquake intensity

Intensity describes the severity of shaking experienced at a particular location. It considers observable effects on people, objects, buildings and the ground.

The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale, developed in its modified form in 1931, contains 12 levels. These are conventionally represented by Roman numerals, beginning with generally imperceptible shaking at level 1 and ending with catastrophic effects at level 12.

Intensity varies from one place to another because it depends on distance from the source, focal depth, local soil and rock conditions, and the vulnerability of structures.

Magnitude versus intensity

AspectMagnitudeIntensity
MeasuresEarthquake sizeLocal shaking severity
BasisInstrumental dataObserved or estimated effects
Spatial variationSource propertyVaries by location
Examples of scalesRichter and moment magnitudeModified Mercalli and MSK

The magnitude of a particular earthquake does not increase or decrease from town to town. Different agencies may, however, report slightly different estimates because they use different instruments, scales or calculation procedures.

A single magnitude 7 earthquake may cause severe damage in a town built on soft sediment while producing weaker effects in a more distant town situated on firm rock. The earthquake has one source magnitude, but the towns experience different intensities.

Prelims focus

  • A seismogram is the record of seismic ground motion.
  • Richter magnitude is logarithmic.
  • An increase of 1 magnitude unit corresponds approximately to 32 times the energy release.
  • Moment magnitude is particularly useful for large earthquakes.
  • Modified Mercalli intensity has 12 levels.
  • Trap: Magnitude and intensity do not measure the same property.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, Earthquake Waves and Measuring Earthquakes; US Geological Survey, Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity; National Centre for Seismology, Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale, last modified 5 April 2022. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
